name: Philosophical syntax and the method of logical analysis
plain_explanation: A great deal of philosophy, Russell suggests, turns out to be about the logical grammar of language -- getting clear on the actual structure of what we are saying so as to avoid being misled by its surface grammar. Some philosophers think this covers all of philosophy; Russell thinks that overstates the case, but grants the method is extremely useful for traditional problems.
precise_definition: The view, advanced most emphatically by Carnap, that a great part of philosophy can be reduced to 'syntax' (used in a wider sense than customary), such that when errors in syntax are avoided, a philosophical problem is either solved or shown to be insoluble; Russell judges this an overstatement but affirms that 'the utility of philosophical syntax in relation to traditional problems is very great,' illustrating it with the theory of descriptions.
why_it_mattered: It defines the school's characteristic method: tackling philosophical problems 'one at a time,' with the 'quality of science rather than of philosophy,' instead of constructing a single all-encompassing system at a stroke.
historical_origin: Associated especially with Carnap among Russell's contemporaries in this chapter.
examples: The theory of descriptions as an example of syntactic analysis dissolving the ancient puzzle of 'existence.'
objections: Russell: 'I think this is an overstatement' to claim all philosophical problems are merely syntactical.
competing_positions: Traditional system-building philosophy, which attempts a single 'block theory of the whole universe' at one stroke
